questions.prompt: Which team has possession now?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 is assigned the puck after interception, so Navy’s attacking routes become recovery routes; if D1 wins it, update.

questions.prompt: Which two concerns follow the interception?
questions.explanation: The new carrier and middle support are immediate threats; repeating attack pattern ignores turnover.

questions.prompt: Arrange one immediate cover response.

options.text: Compare the carrier and inside support threats
Coordinate a reachable defensive response with D1

questions.explanation: Call the turnover, locate both threats and coordinate the response. A call or chosen lane alone does not complete coverage.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a middle cover point after the interception.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy’s net than both Gold attackers. Reassess the carrier and middle support with D1; a point alone does not complete coverage.

questions.prompt: Imagine D1 wins the puck back while Gold 2 remains in the middle. Which call gives the team useful new information?

options.text: D1 has it; Gold 2 is still middle
Keep the original forward passing pattern
Gold 2 is no longer a concern

questions.explanation: The call identifies D1 as the new carrier and Gold 2 as the remaining pressure cue. That updates teammates after the interception without promising a clear outlet. D1 still checks the lane before passing; YOU offer support that fits the new pressure.

questions.prompt: Name one attacking intention you must abandon after the interception.
questions.explanation: The planned forward pass is no longer the job once Gold owns puck, so call turnover and cover nearest lane; if Navy recovers, rebuild from new location.

questions.prompt: Which job is explicitly assigned to YOU?

options.text: Keep the inside lane while D1 pressures the carrier

questions.explanation: YOU are inside Gold 2 while D1 is closer to carrier, so the switch requires inside coverage; if Gold 2 changes lane, call it.

questions.prompt: Which two pieces of information should be called?

options.text: Whether the switch is complete without naming who has Gold 1

questions.explanation: Name the carrier responsibility and Gold 2’s route. A switch is not complete just because someone calls it.

questions.prompt: Arrange one communicated switch.

options.text: Call the carrier and inside threat

questions.explanation: The call creates shared information; D1 pressures when YOU know inside threat; YOU confirm handoff.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the middle while staying closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example places YOU closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2, not with Gold 2 between YOU and the net. Communicate with D1 as either attacker moves.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 cuts behind YOU, what should you do?

options.text: Call the new lane and recover net-side
Stay with the old picture silently

questions.explanation: The cut changes the inside threat, so a clear call and net-side recovery preserve coverage; if D1 takes Gold 2, confirm.

questions.prompt: What makes a switch useful instead of two players chasing one puck?
questions.explanation: The switch names carrier and inside threat, then each defender owns a different lane; if either changes route, communicate and exchange again.

questions.prompt: What is D1 doing after pinching down from the blue line?

options.text: Moving down from the blue line into support

questions.explanation: D1’s pinch commits a player forward past the blue line, so YOU read whether the puck can move away from pressure; if possession is lost, recovery replaces escape.

questions.prompt: Which two cues support a quick wall escape?

options.text: Whether W offers a usable outlet
D2 is standing on the goalie crease

questions.explanation: Check the pressure and possible outlet. D2 can also matter as a reset; no one’s location guarantees an escape.

questions.prompt: Arrange one pinch-escape read.

options.text: Use W only if the passing lane is usable

questions.explanation: D1’s movement changes the support shape. Protect possession where possible and check the outlet before using it.

questions.prompt: Move W nearer the middle while staying closer to the blue line than YOU.
questions.explanation: The example changes W’s passing angle and stays separate from YOU. Check Gold 1, D1 and the route before using the outlet.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 takes away W, what should YOU reassess?

options.text: Whether D2 is safer reset and D1 can recover
Continuing the pinch as if puck were safe

questions.explanation: W’s lane is removed, so scan D2 and D1’s recovery; if neither is available, protect and wait.

questions.prompt: Why does a pinch make the wall support cue more important?
questions.explanation: D1’s activation adds a player but leaves recovery responsibility, so a visible wall outlet lets YOU escape; if it closes, the team resets.

questions.prompt: Which two changes should YOU make?

options.text: Move toward a visible D1 outlet lane
Keep Gold 1 in the pressure scan

questions.explanation: The release changes support side and forechecker remains relevant; staying fixed ignores both cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange one goalie-outlet support change.
questions.explanation: Puck side determines route; showing a lane connects D1; Gold 1 decides whether it is safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the middle to compare an outlet for D1.

questions.explanation: The forechecker removed the first route, so D2 and D1’s protection become the next read; if middle reopens, present again.

questions.prompt: Why does the goalie’s release change your support job?
questions.explanation: The new puck owner and side determine where a short outlet can exist, so move with the play while scanning Gold 1; if contested, support becomes protection.

questions.prompt: What is your current role?

options.text: Third-player support behind F1 and W

questions.explanation: YOU are third behind carrier and support, so height balances attack and recovery; if possession changes, job changes.

questions.prompt: Which two outcomes should your height support?

options.text: A trailing option if F1 keeps control
A route back if Gold wins puck
Joining W in the same lane

questions.explanation: A connected third player supports attack and recovery; joining W removes separation and balance.

questions.prompt: Arrange one third-player read.

options.text: Check F1’s control and Gold 2’s height
Adjust when possession or support changes

questions.explanation: Control and defensive height set risk; a connected trail supports both outcomes; lane changes with puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle while staying behind F1 toward the blue line.
questions.explanation: The example remains separate from F1 and W. Check Gold 2 and the current possession before choosing an outlet or recovery route.

questions.prompt: If F1 loses control, what should YOU do first?

options.text: Use the connected lane to protect middle
Continue deep into the offensive zone
Skate beside W without checking Gold 2

questions.explanation: Turnover makes recovery first; connected middle preserves coverage; if Navy wins it, attack restarts.

questions.prompt: Why is the third player more than a late scoring option?
questions.explanation: The third player connects attack while protecting the turnover route, so height reflects puck control and defensive risk; if play settles, activate.
